newsitem.title: USA: Ben & Jerry's names gun consultant as new CEO.
newsitem.headline: Ben & Jerry's names gun consultant as new CEO.

text.p: Ben & Jerry's Homemade Inc., the iconoclastic ice cream maker, said Thursday that Perry Odak, a former executive of the firm that makes Winchester rifles, would become its new chief executive.

Odak, 51, who has a quarter of a century's experience with a number of manufacturers of consumer products, will succeed Bob Holland, who resigned in September after less than two years as CEO, saying the job should go to someone with more marketing experience.

"I think there's a real opportunity for this company to regain its momentum and move forward despite the (competitive) market," Odak said in a telephone interview from Ben & Jerry's South Burlington, Vt. headquarters.

Odak most recently served as chief operating officer in a consulting capacity for nine months at U.S. Repeating Arms Co., which manufactures sporting rifles and shotguns, a spokesman for the company said.
He also held senior management positions at Dellwood Foods, Armour-Dial, and Jovan Inc. over the past 25 years.
Wall Street greeted the news by sending shares of Ben & Jerry's, which have been battered over the last year, up 62.5 cents to $11.50 in light trading on Nasdaq in early afternoon trading.

Analysts were enthusiastic about Odak's experience, but were surprised that Ben & Jerry's, which donates part of the profits of its "Peace Pops" and other products to anti-handgun organisations, would hire a former consultant to a rifle manufacturer.
"Going from guns to 'Peace Pops' is a pretty drastic step," said one analyst who declined to be identified.

Co-founder and Chairman Ben Cohen, often dressed in t-shirts and jeans at company functions, reportedly disagreed with Holland's decision to sell Ben & Jerry's in France because of that country's decision not to sign a nuclear test-ban treaty.
But he said in an interview Odak's background was not a problem.

"We spent a long time talking about the social mission of the company and Perry is very much aligned with that social mission," Cohen said. "Our company in the past has taken a stance against handgun violence and in favour of handgun control and Perry very much agrees with those stands."
Odak joins a company which has been unsuccessful recently at using its strong brand name to grow.

The super-premium ice cream category has been flat for years as consumers have turned to low-fat and no-fat desserts, and Ben & Jerry's has been losing market share to Grand Metropolitan Plc's Haagen-Dazs.

Ben & Jerry's announced last fall it would report a loss of from 13 cents to 17 cents per share in the seasonally-weak fourth quarter due to competition from Haagen-Dazs and costs from promotions and the expansion into Europe.
In last year's fourth quarter Ben & Jerry's posted a profit of $859,000, or 12 cents per share.

Analysts also questioned Odak's commitment to Ben & Jerry's since he jumped jobs many times in the past. However, Odak said he signed a three-year agreement with the company and, unlike his predecessor, planned to move to Vermont from his home in York, Pa.
Odak declined to talk about Ben & Jerry's plans to grow, but stressed his experience working overseas and with entrepreneurial owners.

"I understand transitions and I believe I am good at working with companies through transitions. This company is going through a transition, being very entrepreneurial to having more of balance ... inside the company," he said.
